https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil protests: activists threaten to slash artworks
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Protesters may emulate suffragette who took a meat cleaver to a Velázquez
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Just Stop Oil could slash famous works of art in a bid to “escalate” their campaign to highlight the dangers of climate change.
Members of the group said they were considering damaging paintings over the next few weeks in imitation of the strategy adopted by the suffragette Mary Richardson, who attacked the Rokeby Venus painting by Diego Velázquez with a meat cleaver after Emmeline Pankhurst, the group’s organiser, was arrested.
This was followed by Anne Hunt, who in the same year smuggled a weapon under her clothes into the National Portrait Gallery and slashed a painting of Thomas Carlyle.
Alex De Koning, speaking to Sky News for JSO, said that the group would “take inspiration from past successful movements” as it called on the government to end all new oil and gas licences.
“We’re going to do everything we can,” he said.
Asked if that included slashing artwork, he replied: “It could potentially come to that at one point in the future, yeah. If that’s unfortunately what it needs to come to, then that’s unfortunately what it needs to come to. We’re fighting for our lives, why would we do any less?”
In October two activists from the group were charged with criminal damage after tomato soup was thrown over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers at the National Gallery in London.
The painting, with an estimated value of £72.5 million, was covered with protective glass so it was unscathed, although there was minor damage to the frame.
Other stunts have included JSO activists gluing themselves to the frame of a John Constable painting and Van Gogh’s 1889 work Peach Trees in Blossom.
In Germany two demonstrators from another climate group threw mashed potatoes at Les Meules by Monet at the Barberini Museum in Potsdam. The painting, also covered in glass, was undamaged and was put back on display days later.
On Monday Just Stop Oil began another sustained period of direct action as they performed slow marches flanked by police through Shepherd’s Bush and the Strand.
The move away from the group’s previous tactics of gluing themselves to roads has been designed to attract new members with methods that are “non injunction breaking” and that “aim to be non-arrestable”.
This week Jan Goodey, 57, from Just Stop Oil was jailed for six months for a protest that caused “mile after mile” of tailbacks on the M25 this month, with the judge saying Goodey had “deliberately set out to disrupt the lives of individuals doing no more than going about their lawful business”.

image.caption: Diego Velázquez’s Rokeby Venus was damaged by a suffragette in 1914UNIVERSAL HISTORY ARCHIVE/GETTY IMAGES

https://www.thetimes.com/article/stirlin.title: Stirling University student union first in UK to ban meat and dairy
https://www.thetimes.com/article/stirlin.subtitle: Campus outlets will serve only plant-based food from 2025
https://www.thetimes.com/article/stirlin.text:
Students at a university that specialises in sporting excellence have become the first in the UK to ban meat and dairy products, sparking claims that it is an “attack on freedom of choice”.
The union at the University of Stirling has committed to serving only plant-based food in campus outlets, and phasing out all forms of animal produce including cheese, cow’s milk and honey, by 2025.
The move was proposed by the Plant-Based Universities (PBU) campaign — an offshoot of the direct action group Extinction Rebellion — and has been supported by Chris Packham, the BBC broadcaster and activist.
A spokesman for PBU said: “Stirling Students’ Union has listened to the scientific advice from world-leading academics and is setting a gold standard in environmental policy for other universities to follow.”
Imogen Robertson, 21, a student campaigner at Stirling, north of Edinburgh and Glasgow, said: “We will be working with catering staff to ensure this vote is implemented in a way that provides cheap, delicious, planet-saving options throughout our students’ union.
“We hope this sparks a wave of bold action across UK universities to commit to just and sustainable plant-based catering.”
The motion was passed last week at a union meeting attended by about 100 people.
The university has a student population of more than 17,000 and its alumni include the Olympic swimmer Duncan Scott, the professional golfers Richie Ramsay and Catriona Matthew, Grace Dent, the food critic and broadcaster, and Lord McConnell of Glenscorrodale, the former Scottish first minister.
Aaron Caulfield, who proposed the motion, added: “I was pushed to bring this motion by the belief that universities should not be hypocritical, and should follow their own research and the research of other institutions.
“It should also help people who would not otherwise be exposed to vegan food to expand their meat-free options within their own diet at home.”
The campus hosts Scotland’s national swimming and tennis centres.
At present union-run outlets sell chicken, burgers and bacon rolls, while its student handbook was previously sponsored by the fast food firm Domino’s and featured images of pepperoni pizzas.
Packham, the host of Springwatch, tweeted his support: “Young people are doing it for themselves. This is good.”
However, the Countryside Alliance claimed the move was illogical and illiberal.
“This is an attack on freedom of choice imposed by a tiny number of students on the wider student body, but it is also illogical,” Mo Metcalf-Fisher, a spokesman for the organisation, said. “Stirling’s students’ union would be much better off sourcing sustainable local meat and dairy produce from Scottish farmers instead. How can an avocado flown in from South America have eco-superiority over a piece of grass-fed beef from a local farm?
“Stirling University should demonstrate their support for Scottish farmers by ensuring they continue to supply meat and dairy, irrespective of what its students’ union decide to do”.
The decision will not affect refectories and cafés run directly by the university.
The University of Edinburgh rejected a similar proposal in a campus-wide referendum in 2020. Of the 6,000 votes cast, 58 per cent said no to imposing veganism in campus cafés and restaurants.

image.caption: Imogen Robertson and Aaron Caulfield were among the Stirling students campaigning for the changeTHE VEGAN AND RIGHTS FOR ANIMALS SOCIETY

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/anti.title: Anti-terror chief accused of ‘woke stunt’ on menopause
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/anti.text:
Britain’s anti-terrorism chief has been accused of carrying out a “woke stunt” after he wore a special jacket that simulates menopausal hot flushes at a police meeting.
Assistant Commissioner Matt Jukes, the Metropolitan Police’s “HeForShe gender equality lead”, wore the “MenoVest” to mark Menopause Awareness Month when he attended the force’s environment and sustainability board.
He said that he found the vest with heated pads uncomfortable and distracting, adding that as the heat came to a peak in waves he had a feeling of, “Oh no, not now” and “an anticipation before really losing my train of thought”.
He said that the jacket had given him heightened awareness of the experiences of menopausal women as he vowed to “redouble my focus to normalise our conversations about the menopause at work”.
The Met’s 33,000 officers were urged to watch an intranet video of Jukes talking about his experience. However, Phil Flower, a former Scotland Yard chief superintendent, criticised him, saying: “Growing public concern about the police’s ability to deal effectively with crime will be further undermined by this woke stunt. Perhaps Matt Jukes could be encouraged to put on a blue uniform next time and walk on the streets at night to understand what it is like to be a real policeman.”
Another retired Scotland Yard chief superintendent, Dai Davies, said: “Mr Jukes should concentrate on arresting burglars and people who attack women to counter the appalling level of arrests and charges in the Met, let alone convictions. He should leave women to be women, and encourage officers to do what they are paid to do: arrest criminals and protect the public.”
The condemnation comes amid widespread criticism of police chiefs across the country for engaging in “woke” gestures.
Suella Braverman, the home secretary, and members of the public have hit out this week at police who did not prevent Just Stop Oil activists repeatedly bringing the M25 to a standstill.
However, Diane Danzebrink, founder of Menopause Support, welcomed the exercise, saying: “It’s important for men to be educated about menopause because they will all know somebody who experiences it.”
In June a scathing inspection report revealed a catalogue of failures by Britain’s biggest force, which did not record tens of thousands of crimes, ignored almost all victims of antisocial behaviour, let down vulnerable victims, and neglected a huge backlog of online child abuse referrals.
Her Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire and Rescue Services announced that “systemic concerns” about the force’s performance were so grave that it needed to be put under special measures.
As assistant commissioner for specialist operations at the Met, Jukes heads the UK’s counterterrorism policing network.
He said: “I make no apologies for spending a fraction of a long working week ensuring women who make a massive contribution to the Met whilst experiencing the menopause feel recognised and supported.”

image.caption: Matt Jukes wore a MenoVest to try to find out what the menopause is likeJOHN SIBLEY/ALAMY

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/article.title: Simon Schama: ‘King Charles could give the monarchy a new lease of life’
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/article.text:
‘I was born to the soundtrack of history during the Nazi rocket attacks,” Simon Schama declares at the opening of his new BBC series. Its title, History of Now, has a deliberate sense of urgency. Schama was born in 1945 and grew up as part of a generation intent on rebuilding the world from the rubble of war. The three-part series explores the role of artists, writers and musicians in fighting for democracy. But as we meet the future looks uncertain. Britain is on its third prime minister in three months. In the US, the election-denying Donald Trump is preparing for another presidential run and Joe Biden is warning that political — and nuclear — Armageddon is closer than we think.
What if the march of freedom is not the norm, but a historical blip? All that was solid in the postwar era is melting into air. “One of the hopes we all had in the 1950s is that World War II had seen off brutal, atavistic nationalism,” Schama, 77, says. “What is worrying and unsettling is that democracy in so many parts of the world is on the back foot.”
History of Now shows Schama popping up at a surprising number of historical events, telling the story of the post-1945 world through culture. He is not just a narrator, but a player — in the style of Zelig, the Woody Allen character who appears next to Hitler, Charlie Chaplin and Pope Pius XI. “You are not going to believe this, but I had to be talked into the personal side,” he says with a laugh. True, I would never have expected Britain’s most exuberant cultural historian to downplay his presence. He has a Tiggerish bounce and flair for drama that has served him well when presenting sweeping television chronicles such as The History of Britain (2000) and Civilisations (2018). At his light-filled contemporary home outside New York, Schama is cheerfulness itself. He has lived in America since the 1980s with his wife, Virginia Papaioannou, who is from California and a distinguished geneticist at Columbia University (turned yoga teacher in retirement). “I’m the low entertainer in the family; she is the hardcore brain,” he says. He has kept his British passport, retains a flat in London and was knighted in 2018. But from his perch in both countries, he keeps a weather eye on gathering storms and has a unique take on the two systems that govern the UK and the US.
Fittingly for a knight of the realm, he believes the Crown is a source of resilience in Britain. “What the monarchy does is provide a space where people can actually belong to a national community and to its history without the bitterness of mutual political hatred.
“The Queen is an almost impossible act to follow, but it helps that Charles’s obsession for the last 30 or 40 years happens to be something that is at the centre of history now, namely the future of the planet.” Schama doubts that our new king has been affected by the revival of his betrayal of Diana in the Netflix drama The Crown. As for Meghan, he says shrewdly: “The Oprah show effect faded quite quickly.”
Schama thinks the royal family is in “as good a condition as you could expect” and King Charles and Prince William could give the monarchy a “new lease of life”.
“Yes, there is money and privilege, and they all live in palaces, but it is completely outweighed by living in presidential America . . . If the next president comes to power on the basis of something that is demonstrably false, that is an incredibly dangerous situation.”
On a global scale, he warns that “gains are not irreversible, that is for sure”. He adds: “The autocratic bet — whether by Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin or Viktor Orban’s illiberal democracy — is that most people don’t really care about democracy or the free press. If you offer them a choice between a vote or a washing machine, they’ll take the washing machine.”
Schama is afraid a “casual wrecking party” is playing fast and loose with our institutions, including the BBC, which has nurtured him for 30 years. “It is absolutely sui generis in broadcasting around the world. I do think abolishing the licence fee would be an awful thing to do,” he says. Its demise would be “catastrophic for the country”.
He takes the long view of events. Schama calls it “part of the historian’s distress”. His progress through the postwar era placed the 13-year-old Schama at a gloomy beach resort in Belgium in 1958. “I had gone on a rain-soaked holiday with the parents of a friend of mine, which was terrible, except there were girls, which made it less terrible,” he recalls. But from there they went on to the Brussels World Fair, where the silver-sphered Atomium promised a shiny, science-based future.
By the mid-1960s he was a student in Czechoslovakia, not long before Russian tanks crushed the Prague Spring. Several people he knew were arrested and thrown in jail. “All my friends were going to Kathmandu to get the perfect weed. But I was interested in this creepy John le Carré-Len Deighton twilight world,” he recalls. Schama went on to celebrate the 1989 Velvet Revolution and returns in the series to the balcony where the playwright and future Czech president Vaclav Havel greeted a jubilant post-Soviet crowd in Wenceslas Square.
He was also a teller at the Cambridge Union in 1965 when James Baldwin, the eloquent novelist and civil rights activist, defeated the sinuous William Buckley, often regarded as the father of American conservatism. The subject of debate was “whether the American dream was at the expense of the American negro”.
“I picked the cotton and carried it to market, I built the railroads under someone else’s whip for nothing. For nothing,” Baldwin said, mesmerising his audience. And — blink and you’ll miss it — the future Sir Simon can be seen on grainy black-and-white film presenting the count.
It was at this point that his producers had a brainwave. “Why don’t we map [the series] against your life?” they asked. Writers, artists and composers are at the heart of Schama’s story. “The worst thing you can do is to prescribe that artists must necessarily engage with history, but they can and do have an effect when they do,” Schama says. They are the truth tellers, whether it is the novelist George Orwell battling to preserve history and memory in Nineteen Eighty-Four (“the Russians calling Ukrainians ‘Nazis’ are exactly what Orwell was talking about”) or Pablo Picasso painting the agony of the bombing of Guernica.
“It is at times like this we realise what great art is truly for,” Schama says. In the series he interviews the exiled Chinese artist Ai Weiwei and the Canadian writer Margaret Atwood, whose 1985 novel The Handmaid’s Tale anticipated the reversal of US abortion rights. (BBC4 will be running 30-minute spin-offs of their interviews.)
Schama regards the twisted metal forged by Ai from the remnants of shoddily constructed schools, where thousands of children died in the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, as a masterpiece. He is in awe of the artist, pointing to a picture of the hole in the ground where Ai lived as a boy after his father, a poet, fell out of favour during the Cultural Revolution. Dictators have to destroy art because “truth and art are so powerful”, Ai tells Schama in the film. “That makes me feel a sense of accomplishment.”
Unlike communist China, the age of populism in the West has yet to produce a creative genius to match Ai. Schama is “not thrilled”, to put it mildly, by the Just Stop Oil protesters who flung soup at Van Gogh’s Sunflowers at the National Gallery and mashed potatoes at Monet’s Haystacks at a German museum in Potsdam. “Are they deliberately choosing the artists who loved nature most? Sunflowers is virtually a pantheist manifesto,” he fumes. “And what has done more than art to make people care more deeply and viscerally about the fate of the Earth? Throw soup at the front door of an oil executive or something.”
Schama’s home near the well-named Pleasantville, 30 miles north of Manhattan, seems far removed from these concerns. The interior is stylish, with panoramic views of the Hudson Valley. His study is crammed with books from floor to ceiling, revealing his restless, energetic mind at work. He spent lockdown researching a book on 18th- and 19th-century vaccines, Foreign Bodies, which will be published in the spring.
“I was being the usual liberal chucklehead, thinking that in the case of a pandemic obviously countries would have to collaborate,” he says. “More idiot me!” Typically for Schama, within the big picture he has identified an extraordinary character — the French literary great Marcel Proust’s father, Adrien, a distinguished epidemiologist. “That made me sit up and take notice.”
Schama was fascinated by a second revelation. The bubonic plague killed 26 million people from 1897 to 1926, but was “completely forgotten” because it occurred almost entirely in Asia, he says. It is a reminder that mankind has emerged from terrible pandemics before and faced down other existential crises. Schama recalls catastrophising about the 1962 Cuban missile crisis as a teenager. “I went home to my parents and said it was their fault I was going to be fried like a crisp. Here was I, Mr Fabulous Teenager, saying, ‘You’ve had your life already.’ My poor parents, the blood drained from their face.”
As a diehard liberal, Schama is impatient with the new censoriousness. “The left is intolerant too. I hate cancelling, which happens on both sides, right and left.” A longtime professor of art history and history at Columbia University, he deplores the vanishing of humanities in universities. “The notion that humanities should be reduced to an optional luxury — an ornamentation — is awful because humanities immerse you in what it is like to be a human being.
He blames the internet for reducing political argument to people “swearing at each other” (although he can dish it out punchily on Twitter). I ask if he worries that our history will be altered or vanish, as in Nineteen Eighty-Four, when we abandon physical records for the impermanence of the “cloud”.
Schama looks puzzled for a moment, then laughs. “You’ve just successfully landed another anxiety on me. Now I’ll have no sleep at all.”
Simon Schama’s History of Now starts next Sunday at 9.15pm on BBC2
AmarcordFederico Fellini, 1973 Although ostensibly autobiography, about Fellini’s boyhood in Rimini, actually all of life is in this movie: the lusty bits, naturally (it’s Fellini), but also tender, manic comedy (small nun in a tall tree); crazed arguments round the family table; the local historian (ah); the pains of taking on the fascists and a vision of a great ocean liner heaving into view, its lights ablaze. All to Nino Rota music.
Blue Poles (Number 11)Jackson Pollock, 1952I’ve always loved Pollock’s weaves of dripped paint. As a boy I would go with my dad to Lancashire loom sheds and see fabric chattering off the machines, half resolving into patterns, so I “got” abstraction early on. This one is literally mesmerising — you’re glassy-eyed in lost contemplation, but then there are those “poles” to hang on to when infinite immersion gets weird.
Used SongsTom Waits, 1973-80He’s the troubadour of ruin, a voice that’s been smoked, brined, shredded in a grater, then roughed up a bit more, all the better to deliver the scenery of worn-out longing, rueful regret, bruised innocence amid dodgy late night diners, infomercials on speed and Ol’ 55, the most rapturous morning-after love song ever.
ArcadiaTom Stoppard, 1993Egotistically, I saw this beautiful, complicated, hilarious, time-tripping play (in both senses of the word) around Enlightenment, science and landscape, in its first weeks when I was writing my book Landscape and Memory and was shaken (in a good way) that my thematic obsessions in the book and Stoppard’s motifs were so connected, if not, in places, exactly the same. Plus there’s dancing and a tortoise.
To the End of the Land David Grossman, 2008The novel that registers most acutely and powerfully the agony of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict; also the obsession with land as a fever dream and actual ground. The most poetically intense of this great writer’s work; with some astounding writing in its opening pages — and as a pack of wild dogs close in...

https://www.thetimes.com/article/north-s.title: North Sea oil: a new black gold rush?
https://www.thetimes.com/article/north-s.text:
Afloat on a hulking orange-painted structure off the Orkney Islands, I am trying to understand what drives people to abandon family, friends and the safety of land to become an oil worker in the North Sea.
The industry has been struggling for the past few years, admits Marc Swinton, 41, from Edinburgh, showing me around the Stena Spey, a 15,000-tonne, six-legged monster anchored in Scapa Flow by eight giant chains with links bigger than dinner plates. “We’ve lost roustabouts, roughnecks, the younger men,” says Swinton, the rig manager, using the industry’s colourful jargon for different deck hands. “The downturn over the past few years with lower oil prices and Covid has been dramatic.”
Tens of thousands of North Sea jobs have been axed and dozens of rigs sliced up and sold for scrap, dismantled in Europe or Turkey or dumped on an Indian beach amid growing public pressure for greener fuel. There is no better symbol of the industry’s woes than the Stena Spey and her skeleton crew of 42, down from 120 when it had been drilling for oil. The rig is currently “hot stacked”, a term meaning crewed but inactive. “It breaks my heart that this rig is sitting here doing nothing,” Swinton says.
That may soon change: The Sunday Times Magazine has been granted exclusive access to this rust-stained hulk towering 250ft above the waves just as the government is in the process of approving licences for up to 130 new oil and gas exploration projects in response to the energy crisis.
Environmental campaigners say the offer of new leases is like funnelling whisky into a recovering alcoholic: it will trigger a relapse into the bad old carbon-pumping behaviour of the past. It has prompted attacks by climate protesters from Last Generation and Just Stop Oil, who have defaced museum masterpieces by Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh. At the Museum Barberini in Potsdam, Germany, a female activist shouted that the world was in “a climate catastrophe and all you are afraid of is tomato soup or mashed potatoes on a painting”. Others argue that besides promoting climate change the new drilling will not bring down our energy bills, let alone make us any less dependent on foreign suppliers such as Russia.
“It can take decades to get from exploration to the stage where oil comes out of the ground,” says Tessa Khan, founder of Uplift, an organisation campaigning for a fossil fuel-free UK. “The new licensing is not going to lower energy bills or shore up our energy security any time soon.” Nevertheless, the whiff of new opportunity has put a spring back in the step of the Stena Spey’s remaining roughnecks and roustabouts, who hope the dinosaur industry can be lifted out of the doldrums and that their rig will get in on the action.
The prospect stirs memories of an exciting heyday of high salaries, flashy cars and rowdy nightclubs, when offshore work was considered glamorous and roughnecks earning hundreds of pounds a day threw them around with abandon in the boom oil city of Aberdeen. In those days rig crews were rewarded with champagne breakfasts and medals inscribed “oil finder” if and when they struck the “black gold”. On the Stena Spey the men received glass vials containing the first oil samples as keepsakes.
In recent years the search for oil has been brought to a virtual standstill: only five wells were drilled for exploration last year — the lowest number ever. Self-sufficient in oil and gas in 2004, Britain has become an importer — unlike Norway, a rich global energy provider on the other side of the North Sea.
The downturn might have spelt doom for the Stena Spey, delivered in 1983 and, arguably, close to the end of her career. She could have been “left for the razorblades”, as a crew member referred to the fate of old rigs cut up for scrap. Instead the Stena Spey has kept busy, branching into decommissioning work, itself a multibillion-pound industry in which drilling technology is redirected into restoring the seabed to its original state. Hundreds of wells and surface platforms dating back to the 1960s and classed as no longer economically viable have been abandoned. They must all be decommissioned along with other infrastructure, from pipelines to terminals.
Some of this work “may become urgent”, Swinton says. “It will take only one well to go bad for there to be an incident,” he adds, referring to the dangers of oil leaking out into the sea. “And I would hate for that to happen. Let’s be proactive rather than sitting here doing nothing.”
At the same time Swinton, who now works mostly onshore, sounds nostalgic for his days searching for oil. “It’s an unbelievable feeling. There’s nothing quite like the thrill of finding oil,” he says, his eyes lighting up as he describes a stint in the Gulf of Mexico in 2012. After reaching 26,000ft under the seabed, which took weeks and tens of millions of dollars, the team was about to give up empty-handed when a geologist insisted they drill down a little further. “So we drilled another 10ft. And then we found it — boom, gold! It was a huge find,” Swinton says. The drill site, called Pony, was renamed Stampede.
Unlike America’s Republicans, who adopted “Drill, baby, drill!” as their 2008 campaign slogan, Chris Carbaugh, from Maryland, a senior executive at Stena Drilling, is trying not to sound too excited about the new “blocks” being offered for drilling in the North Sea. “I don’t think we’re going to see us going from zeros to heroes overnight,” he says. “It’s not going to be like that. More like a resurgence.”
The announcement, though, is “a real boost to morale”, he says. “We’ve been working at a loss for the past few years. We’re very hopeful that some of the operators who gain these leases will need rigs for the work.”
So should we try to make the most of our remaining reserves — estimated at about 15 billion barrels of oil — in pursuit of greater energy security? And can enough workers be tempted back to the oil rigs, once considered the best-paying blue-collar employment on the eastern coast of the UK but now part of a “sunset” industry?
“There are no graduates coming in, that’s for sure,” laments Dillan Perras, director of Stena Wells, another of the Swedish company’s satellites. “The older guys are retiring and there’s no one who wants to replace them. We’ve lost a huge amount of experience.”
Andrew Morrison, “master”, or captain of the Stena Spey, adds: “The younger generation has grown up with the idea that hydrocarbons are bad … but we’ll still need this form of energy for some time to come.”
For Paul Murray, 47, a “senior toolpusher”, or drilling director, who has spent most of his working life on oil rigs, this is all part of a “boom to bust” cycle he has seen before. “We’ve been in a long bust period and now we’re coming out the other end and another boom is on the horizon,” he predicts as he looks out across Scapa Flow, where the German fleet was scuttled at the end of the First World War. “There’s a boom followed by a decline,” Murray adds, “then a rise in the oil price, with more licensing and ‘We’re good, let’s go again’, they say, ‘We need to attract people, let’s put their salaries up.’ It’s all starting again.”
I am accompanied on the half-hour boat ride from Orkney to the rig by Stena executives as well as representatives of Offshore Energies UK — formerly Oil and Gas UK — and Kenneth Gibson, an SNP member of the Scottish parliament. We have to climb metal steps that zigzag up one of the rig’s six giant legs. The platform itself is topped by an Eiffel Tower-shaped derrick as tall as Nelson’s Column. Under this is the “dog house”, a cabin from where the drill is controlled. There I meet George McDougall, 54, another “toolpusher” and one of the longest-serving crew. It was the money, he admits, that got him “roughnecking on wells” a quarter of a century ago. “The wife was pregnant, we had twins, we needed more income. There was good money to be made out here.” The twins, a boy and a girl, are now grown up and employed in the industry — McDougall’s son offshore and his daughter in an office in Aberdeen.
We are surrounded by display screens and instrument panels and dressed in white hard hats, red jumpsuits, protective gloves and glasses. I feel like an extra in a Bond villain’s secret lair. Safety requirements on oil rigs have tightened over the years after a series of accidents, including an explosion that caused the Piper Alpha platform to sink in 1988 with the loss of 167 lives. Physical injuries used to be common, with fingers lost in the “rig tong” — a giant wrench — or workers crushed under falling machinery.
“Thirty years ago they’d celebrate just two weeks without a serious injury requiring time off,” says Morrison, 36. And although the Stena Spey boasts of being accident-free for years, “working offshore is still a dangerous occupation”, he says. “The potential for mishaps is huge if things aren’t managed well.”
Our first stop is a conference room for a demonstration of the various alarms we might hear if we’re unlucky. The most strident is an invitation to abandon ship. Two life rafts, each able to carry 60 people, are perched on a railing 100ft above the sea.
It may come as no surprise that on top of safety hazards, oil rigs can take a toll on family life. Like all the others, Morrison, whose father also worked in the industry and once spent two years away from home in one stretch, must work three weeks at sea continuously. He then gets three weeks off, which he spends at home with his wife, a physiotherapist. They have a seven-year-old daughter and an 18-month-old son, and live in the Outer Hebrides. “I’ve missed five birthdays and five Christmases,” Morrison says with a rueful smile as he shows me around his quarters. They consist of a bunk, writing desk, television and shower, a bit like the best cabins on cross-Channel ferries.
Modern communications have helped to overcome the pain of separation but video calls can complicate matters. “I’ve seen guys punching the wall,” one crew member tells me. “There’s nothing they can do when their girlfriend’s all dressed up and tells them they’re about to go out on the town.”
Reports over the years suggest that oil workers experience greater anxiety and depression than those on “the beach” — industry lingo for a land-based posting. Several decks below Morrison’s quarters is a gym, where one of the crew is blowing off steam, pounding away on a treadmill.
Murray, the toolpusher from Fife, has had long years of juggling his family and professional life. “When you go home for three weeks, you can’t be selfish and take all that time for yourself,” he says. “You have to make sure you take your share of the family’s roles, responsibilities and burdens.”
Alcohol is forbidden on the rig but other hazards, according to anecdotal evidence, used to include obesity. I understand why when we head off to lunch in the canteen. We are faced with an impressive array of cold meats, salads and hot dishes including “chicken Balmoral”, a bacon and mushroom-infused concoction in honour of the late Queen. There is also a colourful variety of puddings and ice creams. The 32-year-old chef, Rob Dasey from Middlesbrough, admits that this is not the average, daily fare. “Once every trip we’ll do a special meal, push the boat out a bit,” he explains.
I sit next to Gibson, the SNP politician. The party’s leader, Nicola Sturgeon, Scotland’s first minister, has a partnership with the Greens at Holyrood and last year condemned Shell’s project to pump 170 million barrels over the next 25 years from a deep oilfield called Cambo, 75 miles northwest of Shetland, one of the largest untapped fields in the North Sea. Shell pulled out of the deal, which had been expected to create 1,000 jobs. It conspired against the government’s climate compatibility “checkpoints” as well as a pledge made by Boris Johnson ahead of last year’s climate summit in Glasgow to make Britain carbon net neutral by 2050.
In a sign of how much things have changed since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Britain has now included Cambo in a list of oil projects to be “fast-tracked”. And the SNP’s opposition to harvesting fossil fuels from the ancient mudstone beneath the North Sea also appears to have softened.
“I feel there’s an argument to be made … to continue producing oil and gas from our waters in an environmentally sustainable way,” Gibson tells me as we tuck into the chicken Balmoral. “It’s not a sunset industry when over 70,000 Scottish people work in it.” The transition to renewables is inevitable — a matter of time, he believes, “for climatic reasons and also because oil is a non-renewable resource — it’s going to run out at some point. At the same time, Scotland has a very high skill base in terms of professionalism and engineering know-how in this sector. We’ve got to make sure we retain these skills with a just transition over a realistic time period.
“I watched Frozen Planet and I saw the ice melting and sea levels rising, and the first thing on the BBC this morning was about coastal erosion. But we’re still putting diesel and petrol into our cars. We’re still using oil in our plastics and other industries. So we have to think, in terms of energy supply, do we want those resources to come from Scotland or elsewhere? Relative to Nigeria or the Gulf of Mexico, there’s a strong argument that oil and gas extraction here is more environmentally sound.”
Sitting opposite Gibson is Perras, the Stena Wells executive, who chips in with an attack on Just Stop Oil, an increasingly vociferous protest movement against new exploration. “Just Stop Oil want us to quit now, turn everything off, but there’s no way the world can function with that type of philosophy,” says Perras, who is from northern Alberta in Canada and has drilled all over the world, including in Peru’s Amazon rainforest. “We have to transition with technology, with infrastructure — and with a change of culture and lifestyle. Telling northern Europe that you can’t fly to southern Europe for your summer holidays would need a culture change,” he says.
The Stena Spey’s orange-painted pontoons are encrusted with barnacles and “yes”, admits Swinton, the manager, “if you look behind the cracks, there’s rust, there are areas to be spruced up”. Otherwise, he insists, she’s “immaculate” and ready for action. First, though, she must undergo her five-yearly technical inspection, an MoT for oil rigs. I’m told it could take a few weeks. And like everything else in the oil business it is extremely expensive, in the region of £30 million.
“We’re organising to do it early enough so that when the summer drilling months begin, the Spey will be ready to hit the ground running,” says Carbaugh, the chief operations officer for Stena Drilling.
Back on deck later I meet Graeme McPherson, the barge master, who has worked on the rig for 15 years. I notice writing tattooed on the top of his chest. “I’m going on a journey to a city fair and bright”, reads the first line of what might be an appropriate prayer for the Stena Spey.
McPherson tells me the poem of unknown origin was written on a card that had meant a lot to his father, who had it by his bedside when he died earlier this year. “We put the card in his suit pocket in the coffin and it was buried along with him.”

image.caption: The rig at anchor off the Orkney IslandsSTEVE MORGAN FOR THE SUNDAY TIMES MAGAZINE

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Here’s an idea: pay people not to do something and thus save the planet
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
On Tuesday the global population hit eight billion. Putting aside the fishy coincidence that this milestone was declared by the United Nations as world leaders were gathering to discuss climate change in Egypt, it is an eye-popping number. In my lifetime, the number of people on this planet has exactly doubled.
Have those four billion extra people made the world a fundamentally worse or better place? Many in Extinction Rebellion support the view of James Lovelock, the scientist who believed climate change and population growth were “two sides of the same coin”, that all these extra bodies had consumed more resources and emitted more carbon. The only solution, they argue, is to slash the world’s population (Lovelock thought it would stabilise, after a mass extinction, at about one billion) or for the existing population to consume much, much less. This is an argument that puts you not just into Liz Truss’s anti-growth camp but into Greta Thunberg’s “eco-death cult”, as her critics have called the Swede’s movement.
How do we square the circle of reducing carbon emissions while not extinguishing growth? I don’t know. But this week a fascinating experiment has started, which gives me hope that it is possible to create economic activity from reducing consumption.
For years the National Grid ESO, or electricity system operator, has persuaded large factories to use less power at peak times. If you are in charge of ensuring the lights stay on, you don’t want a vast brickmaking plant to fire up its kilns at the same time as the country rushes to boil the kettle after England lose a penalty shootout.
This winter it is testing what it calls a demand flexibility service, a scheme to persuade consumers — not just businesses — to use less energy at particular times. On Tuesday it was between 5pm and 6pm, that moment when children are home from school, parents return from work (or close the door on their home office), turn on the oven and set off the dishwasher. Tuesday was the first of 12 of these events. To take part you have to be a customer of Octopus, E.On or a handful of small-fry providers; you also need a smart meter. Octopus invited 1.4 million of its customers to sign up and 400,000 have done so.
Here comes the clever part. In return for the inconvenience of not being able to turn on your oven, washing machine and tumble dryer for a couple of hours, you will be paid. Actual hard cash. Not much — between about £2 and £6, depending on how much you reduce your energy consumption compared with your average usage, which can be worked out thanks to your smart meter.
What is exciting is that you can earn money from not doing something, or at least from doing something you might have done anyway. I am fascinated by incentive schemes and how an illogically small amount of money can make you disproportionately happy.
In recent weeks I have been testing a cashback scheme called JamDoughnut. I bought a fancy toaster from Argos for £163 (Dualit, if you’re wondering) and in return I got £7.74 credited to my bank account within a couple of minutes. Now, of course, Argos (or, indeed, this third-party app) could have marketed the toaster with a 4.74 per cent discount or simply sold it to me for £155.26. But neither of those would have felt like a substantial saving. Having real money arrive into your bank account feels like you’ve won the lottery, when in fact you’ve spent a stupid amount on a toaster.
My reward was not a voucher to spend in Argos, which is how these schemes often work, it was cash. H&M, the Swedish fashion chain, has stopped an impressive 106,000 tonnes of clothes from ending up in landfill since 2013 by giving customers a £5 voucher if they donate a shopping bag’s worth of unwanted clothes in its stores. It’s a simple and clever idea, but arguably — if you were in Greta Thunberg’s camp — it encourages yet more consumption of fast-fashion.
With sky-high energy bills, we should all have a huge incentive to not consume as much electricity this winter. We shouldn’t need a reward scheme, but National Grid and its partners anticipate that a payment of a mere £2 might be enough to persuade millions to use their microwave rather than their oven on certain days of the week.
We know it should work because a similar scheme has been running in California and Texas for several years. It has been run by a third-party broker called OhmConnect, which sells what it calls “negawatt hours” (as in, negative megawatt hours) to energy companies, guaranteeing them they will not need to fire up expensive, short-term power plants at peak times. It then splits the difference with its consumers, who ended up with what the co-founder, Matt Duesterberg, describes as “beer money”. He’s evangelical about the idea that we, consumers, have a latent value — the electricity we potentially consume — and we should monetise this. In a recent interview, he was asked, apart from energy, what should we pay people not to do and he simply replied: “Fly.”
OhmConnect’s income is generated by the savings made by power companies; it’s unclear who would fund people to not fly, or, indeed, to give up smoking, ditch an unnecessary shopping trip to H&M or to not buy a late-night Big Mac. But there is a sophisticated market in carbon credits; could there not be one in negative consumption?
New challenges always produce new markets. There is potentially an intriguing future whereby cutting back on consumption could be a growth industry, not an anti-growth one.
Harry Wallop is a consumer journalist and broadcaster. Follow him on Twitter @hwallop

https://www.thetimes.com/article/mark-ro.title: Met chief Mark Rowley: There’s no magical way of fixing the force — I have to hit it head-on
https://www.thetimes.com/article/mark-ro.text:
In the past two years, as Scotland Yard endured more scandal than the average institution faces in two decades, many senior police officers concluded that Britain’s biggest force was simply impossible to lead.
For Sir Mark Rowley, however, it was a chance for revolution.
“You’ve got to be bold,” he says, at his modern but bare seventh floor office overlooking the Thames, a stone’s throw from the Palace of Westminster. Metres away the Metropolitan Police’s most senior officers buzz around the open-plan building, working on dozens of tasks set by the new boss in the first two months.
Rowley, 58, immediately set a different tone to his defensive predecessor, Dame Cressida Dick.
He chided officers for lacklustre interactions with the public, announced a beefed-up countercorruption command, declared sexist banter a sackable offence and outlined plans to get more officers chasing criminals and attending every burglary.
Today, dressed in full uniform, he is softly spoken but there is a hint of steel in his tone as he announces reforms to make the Met “match-fit” and restore its reputation. Rowley is concerned that only 90 per cent of the Met’s 35,000 officers are fully deployable, with some 3,000 underperforming or on long-term sick leave. He is frustrated at the “reluctance” in the public sector to dismiss workers who do not pass muster, and wants a change in regulations to remove some of them.
Rowley chooses his words carefully, knowing they could put him at loggerheads with the Police Federation, the powerful organisation that represents rank-and-file officers.
• Met chief: It should be easier to sack police
The Met will always be “super helpful and sympathetic” to officers injured on duty or suffering mental health problems. He adds: “We can’t deal with a workforce where such a big proportion are not properly deployable. Many of these people, they can’t work shifts, or they can’t work many hours in a day, or they can only have limited contact with the public, maybe because of anxiety-related issues.
“There does come a point that, if you can’t be match fit to be a police officer, then it’s challenging for us in that it’s a large number of people we can’t properly deploy.”
Frustration clearly bubbling below his affable surface, he also wants greater powers to sack rogue officers given the systemic failures to tackle misconduct: “I’m just so, so angry about the decisions that have been made on some of these cases ... that has undercooked the response.”
A key priority is addressing misogyny, violence and misconduct, and he plans retrospective investigations into officers who have attracted serial complaints in the past but escaped proper sanction.
“You can’t have second bites at the same cherry, but you might be able to find a new cherry to bite at.
“We are looking at data and intelligence about officers and staff that might give us new opportunities on that same cohort of people. And the resetting of standards is going to ratchet up our response.”
Rowley is keenly aware that historic lows in crime-solving rates are badly damaging public trust, and wants to divert officers from mental health and social work to free up their time for investigations. He will give the NHS and social care agencies a specific deadline, and then start to withdraw officers from those tasks.
He has also pledged to “reinvent” the way the Met investigates fraud and online crimes. With only one in 200 frauds leading to criminal charges, Rowley bemoans the police’s “Woolworths service in an Amazon age”.
Alone, each of these issues is gargantuan, but Rowley is ebullient in the face of the challenge.
“There’s not a magical way of doing this, you’ve got to be bold. If we’re going to bounce out of the steady decline in trust, and sort out some of the issues that are plaguing us, then I have to be very head-on about it.”
Rowley chokes on his coffee in laughter, or perhaps alarm, as I remark on the obstacles of bringing about police reform — that the annual chiefs conference last week felt like Groundhog Day. There were pledges of action, but it sometimes feels glacial.
He says diplomatically: “There are some challenges for policing nationally in keeping up with the pace of change of criminality and society.”
The Met was plunged into crisis last year after the abduction, rape and murder of Sarah Everard by a serving officer, and the outpouring of complaints of misogyny, racism and other misconduct that followed. It was also labelled institutionally corrupt by an independent inquiry into an unsolved murder and placed into special measures.
Rowley spent six years as a senior officer at the Met, but watched its decline from the outside, having missed out on the top job to Dick in 2017 when he was the national head of counterterrorism.
He retired from policing and embarked on a string of strategic private sector contracts, including work for the centre-right think tank Policy Exchange, which has close ties to the government.
As the Met lurched from scandal to scandal, Rowley was penning a detective novel, trekking to Everest base camp and indulging his love of yoga in the foothills of Kathmandu.
He has joked that the decision to leave his comfortable lifestyle and take the helm of the beleaguered force has led “more than one person to question my sanity”.
But it was no surprise to those who know him well that Rowley was first to put the application in when Dick was forced to resign over revelations that officers at Charing Cross had joked about raping colleagues and killing black children.
Ever the optimist, he firmly believes the Met is made up of a “heroic, determined” majority and that the force will bounce back with the right leadership and reforming approach.
His first nine weeks have been a whirlwind, like “Tigger on speed” according to one colleague, affectionately referring to Rowley’s nickname when he was chief constable of Surrey.
• Comment: Crisis in policing is a question of character
The commissioner has popped up all over the force with unannounced visits to custody suites, specialist units and even the headquarters’ running club, allowing him to indulge in a favourite pastime along the Thames while getting the lowdown from the rank and file.
There is purpose behind the whistlestop tour: Rowley wants to get to grips quickly with the failings that led to the Met being placed in special measures in the summer. The litany of shortcomings highlighted by Her Majesty’s inspectors included a failure to record nearly 70,000 crimes, lengthy delays in answering 999 calls, and poor supervision of some investigations.
Rowley knows he has to implement swift change if, like Stephen Watson, the “back to basics” chief who recently rescued Manchester from special measures, he can bring the Met out of the doldrums within 18 months.
The change to police regulations to make it easier to get rid of underperforming officers will be controversial, but he believes it is essential. Of the 3,500 officers who cannot be fully deployed, about 500 are suspended or on limited duties because they are under investigation for serious misconduct, but the remaining 3,000 are poor performers or have long-term health issues.
Rowley wants the government to change regulations so he can overcome the “heavily bureaucratic” process to remove officers. He notes only six were dismissed last year for poor performance.
He has also asked Suella Braverman, the home secretary, to change how officers accused of the most serious wrongdoing are dealt with. He claims his hands are tied under the present system in which most gross misconduct hearings are independently chaired by legal representatives.
• Leading article: Bad Cops
When an independent review by Baroness Casey of Blackstock lambasted an “anything goes” culture of sexism and misconduct, Rowley acknowledged that hundreds of officers and staff should have been thrown out for “disgraceful behaviour”.
Among the most egregious cases was an officer accused 11 times of misconduct including sharing explicit images of himself, sexual harassment, fraud and assault. He has been arrested and received two formal sanctions, but still works for the Met.
As well as improving public confidence by raising standards, Rowley wants a significant improvement in criminal investigations and solve rates.
He has already vowed to send an officer to every burglary and launched Operation Tenacity, a scheme to arrest hundreds of robbers and violent offenders in his first 100 days in office.
A Cambridge maths graduate who used to take his notes on graph paper, Rowley is a big believer in the importance of data and emerging technology, and wants the Met to use it to better understand the scale of sex predators and other violence.
Improving the fight against online crime is also a priority as there is a “massive amount to catch up on” when it comes to fraud, with detection rates at less than 1 per cent.
Coupled with a threefold increase in rape complaints and demands to tackle acquisitive crime, Rowley faces more demand than he has resources. But only one in five calls to the police involves crime, with large amounts of officer time taken up with mental health calls and related issues best tackled by other public agencies.
Rowley plans to lay down the gauntlet to the NHS, social care and mental health services, and insist they take on that burden. Met officers are spending an average of 14 hours in emergency departments looking after people in mental health crisis, and executing warrants on behalf of the NHS for people who need to be sectioned because of fears they could turn violent.
Rowley will give the other public bodies a date when he plans to turn off police support: “It’s never going to be 100 per cent, but we need to start to cut off some of the other things because we’re not doing a good enough job with crime and that’s our core job.”
The environmental protesters who have blockaded the capital’s streets are another huge drain on time — in October alone more than 7,900 officer shifts were diverted to respond to Just Stop Oil disruption. Rowley insisted that the Met was doing all it could to quickly remove protesters, noting that 20 of the ringleaders were in custody.
There were public barbs from Braverman, however, who warned chiefs they were losing public confidence because of an “institutional reluctance” to quickly remove protesters
Rowley is sanguine about the “muck and bullets and individual bumps in the road” that come with the political territory. So far he has enjoyed strong support from his masters Braverman and Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, and they need him to succeed.
“The willingness and support from both City Hall and the Home Office is very strong. We all want the Met to succeed, and we want policing to succeed, so I think that gives you an opportunity. The general picture is of support which is really, really helpful.”
Dick was the fourth commissioner in a row to resign under a cloud, and Braverman and Khan will recognise that a fifth could permanently damage public trust as well as raise serious questions about their judgment. If their support continues, and the reform agenda lands, Rowley has a shot at being the first commissioner to emerge with his reputation intact since Lord Stevens of Kirkwhelpington in 2005.

image.caption: Sir Mark Rowley inside the Met's special operations room in Lambeth. In his first nine weeks in charge he has been making unannounced visits to custody suites and specialist units as part of a drive to raise standardsTIMES PHOTOGRAPHER RICHARD POHLE

https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.title: Climate activists target Beethoven concert in Hamburg
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.subtitle: Last Generation glue their hands to conductor’s stand
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.text:
Climate protesters hijacked a Beethoven concert at one of Germany’s grandest venues by glueing themselves to the conductor’s podium and lecturing the audience about global warming.
The stunt on Wednesday evening at the €866 million Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg was the latest in a string of attention-grabbing antics from Last Generation, a group of radical campaigners whose members have previously thrown substances over paintings by Monet and Klimt.
Minutes before the state orchestra of Saxony was to strike up the first notes of Beethoven’s Violin Concerto in D major, an unidentified man and woman in fluorescent vests clambered on to the stage and stuck their hands to the stand with fast-drying glue, which induced groans from members of the audience.
In a brief speech the woman warned that there would be no more concerts in Hamburg if the low-lying port city were to be submerged beneath rising waters. “If we do nothing now, we will be complicit in the greatest catastrophe humanity has ever suffered,” she said. “Just as there is only one Beethoven violin concerto, we only have this one planet, whose boundaries we’re abusing so badly that catastrophes caused by climate change are getting more frequent and deadly.”
She added: “I always wanted to have children but now I’m so afraid to place a child in this world and look on as it dies in a war over resources or water.”
The pair were swiftly removed and arrested by police officers and the concert resumed.
Last Generation has borrowed many of its tactics from British counterparts such as Insulate Britain and Just Stop Oil. While its activists have obtained plenty of airtime, this has not necessarily furthered their cause. A fortnight ago they were heavily criticised after two members of the movement blocked Berlin’s inner-city ring road, holding up a fire brigade vehicle that was hurrying to the rescue of an injured cyclist, who later died.
Even politicians from the German Green party have said that the protests are a distraction from serious debate about how to cut carbon emissions.
A poll for Der Spiegel found that 86 per cent of Germans felt the campaigners were going too far and 78 per cent supported tougher criminal penalties for stunts such as stopping traffic or daubing mashed potato over the protective glass casings of famous artworks, as in the case of Monet’s Les Meules at the Barberini museum in Potsdam, west of Berlin.

image.caption: The man and woman from Last Generation performed the stunt at Elbphilharmonie, one of the grandest classical music venues in Germany

https://www.thetimes.com/article/germany.title: Germany considers crackdown on eco-activists after death of cyclist
https://www.thetimes.com/article/germany.text:
The Bundestag will debate a crackdown on radical eco-activists as opposition MPs warn that the more militant groups could resort to “climate terrorism” if they are left unchecked.
In recent days the more combative elements of the movement have alienated even their own supporters during a campaign of civil disobedience, including a motorway blockade that allegedly held up a fire brigade vehicle on its way to a dying cyclist.
Inspired by British groups such as Insulate Britain and Just Stop Oil, a German organisation called the Resistance of the Last Generation has attempted to sabotage oil pipelines, cut off access roads to large airports and thrown mashed potato at the glass protecting a painting by Monet in Potsdam.
In response the centre-right Christian Democratic Union and its Bavarian affiliate, the Christian Social Union (CSU), have drawn up a bill that would grant police substantially greater powers against the activists.
These include mandatory minimum prison sentences for damaging or destroying “cultural artefacts” and for obstructing emergency vehicles. Police officers would also be able to pre-emptively arrest protesters if there is a reasonable suspicion that they are on the brink of reoffending.
Some of the proposals echo elements of a broader plan set out last month by Suella Braverman, the British home secretary, who is also seeking to criminalise protests targeting critical infrastructure.
Alexander Dobrindt, the CSU leader in the Bundestag, said the measures were intended to prevent the emergence of a “climate RAF”, alluding to the Red Army Faction. The left-wing extremist group, also known as the Baader-Meinhof gang, have been held responsible for at least 30 deaths during a campaign of terror from the early 1970s to the 1990s.
The bill is likely to be rejected by the ruling coalition but all three of its members, including the German Green party, have expressed frustration with what one senior liberal MP described as the “ever-progressing radicalisation of parts of the climate movement”.
Ricarda Lang, joint leader of the Greens, said talk of terrorism was hysterical but added: “When a protest results in people talking only about the form of the protest rather than the issue [behind it], then this has done a disservice to the issue.”
This week a poll for the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper found that 86 per cent of German voters believed the Last Generation’s actions were doing more harm than good in the struggle against climate change. Only 7 per cent said the group was making a positive contribution.
Two of its members are under criminal investigation after they blocked one of Berlin’s main ring roads, creating a traffic jam that delayed a specialist rescue vehicle that was dispatched to help a cyclist who had been crushed by a concrete mixer.
Firefighters were able to free the cyclist with improvised tools but she later died from her injuries. Franziska Giffey, the city’s mayor, condemned the protest and said it was the eighteenth time that climate activists had stopped the emergency services from reaching their destination on time.
Today another group of Last Generation protesters scaled the Brandenburg Gate, one of Berlin’s most prominent landmarks, and unfurled a banner urging the government to provide “survival for us all”.

image.caption: A Resistance of the Last Generation activist glued his hand to a road during a protest in BerlinFILIP SINGER/EPA

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/last.title: Climate activists throw oil over Gustav Klimt painting in Vienna
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/last.text:
Climate campaigners have thrown oil over a painting by Gustav Klimt hanging in a Vienna museum, the latest in a series of acts of vandalism against famous works of art.
Activists from Last Generation, a movement based in Germany and Austria, filmed themselves spraying a viscous black liquid over the glass case around Klimt’s Death and Life in a protest against new oil and gas drilling, which they described as a “death sentence for humanity”.
Amid cries of condemnation from other visitors in the Leopold museum, one of the protesters then glued his hand to the casing. His companion shouted as he was bundled away by a security guard: “We have to act at last. The planet is dying. Stop this destruction. We are speeding into climate hell.”
The protester who sprayed the black fluid, identified as Florian Wagner, 30, has said it was in fact a “non-toxic fake oil” that he smuggled into the museum in a Thermos.
The painting, completed in 1916 during Klimt’s “golden phase”, is now being inspected by the museum’s curators, while several rooms were closed to the public. “We can only hope that the picture hasn’t been damaged,” it said.
Hans-Peter Wipplinger, the Leopold museum’s director, said: “The concerns of climate activists such as the Last Generation are justified, but attacking artworks is definitely the wrong way to achieve their goal ... Museums are institutions of preservation and in that sense they are a textbook example of sustainability.”
The stunt appears to have been primarily directed at the Austrian oil and gas conglomerate OMV, which had sponsored free entry to the museum today and is contemplating a new gas project in the Weinviertel region of Austria.
The attack was swiftly castigated by parts of the Austrian press. Exxpress, a tabloid, described it as an “attack on our art and our identity” by “climate terrorists”. Thomas Mayer, a prominent journalist for Der Standard, said it was “time to talk about the totalitarian approach and the destructiveness of these self-avowed ‘world-saviours’”.
Inspired by British groups such as Just Stop Oil and Insulate Britain, Last Generation’s attention-grabbing methods have been widely criticised in Germany and even disowned by leaders of the German Green party, who say such actions distract from serious debate about climate change.
Last month Last Generation members poured instant mashed potato mix over Claude Monet’s Les Meules at the Barberini museum in Potsdam, west of Berlin. Two of their peers then blocked one of Berlin’s main inner-city ringroads, delaying a fire brigade vehicle racing to the rescue of a cyclist crushed by a concrete mixer. The cyclist later died.
